name: Koh Ker paired outlets
summary: A large spillway and laterite-walled chute that let water out of the reservoir at Koh Ker, a tenth-century Khmer capital; erosion suggests destructive flows.
description: The weir’s large spillway and laterite-walled chute, described as a pair of water outlets.
tier_reason: Paired outlets can be fine detail; distinct hydraulic functions and deliberate component links defeat automatic merger with the whole weir. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

impact.note: Two outlets of one failed dam, a detail of that single structure, changing nothing lasting and with nothing later resting on them.

date.label: by c. 950 CE (inferred)
date.basis: The authors attribute the two outlets to the capital-period weir probably built 928–941 CE; completion and operation remain approximate.

events.statement: The surviving main spillway and chute are interpreted as having carried reservoir outflow; erosion and displaced laterite indicate water passage, probably including destructive flows.
events.population: Koh Ker builders and users of the capital’s road and water infrastructure
events.caveats: The paper interprets flow from erosion, displaced blocks and hydraulic modeling; the separate timing, routine service and hydraulic performance of each outlet are uncertain. Failure may have occurred soon after construction and exact named operators are unknown.

evidence.supports: Describes the capital-period weir, roadway, spillway and chute.
Reports displaced spillway blocks and eroded chute blocks; interprets historic water discharge and failure, not an individually dated commissioning.
